To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the deep belief network model can be used for learning hierarchical structure in data, and (ii) the model is capable of learning features that are similar to those in V2, and in fact, matches the biological results quantitatively in some cases.

we have developed a sparse deep belief net model that learns a hierarchical structure from unlabeled visual data, and that it learns features that are similar to the receptive fields in the visual area V2 of the cortex.
we develop an unsupervised model for learning deep structure from unlabeled input data, and we demonstrate that the first two layers of the learned model are similar to V1 and V2 respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: 1) Can a hierarchical model learn the statistics of natural images? 2) Can it learn a representation that matches the known properties of V1 and V2? 3) Can we learn the statistics of higher-order correlations?

developing a hierarchical model of the visual cortex that can learn the complex structure present in natural images.

our model is able to learn a hierarchical representation of visual data, which matches well with the known properties of V1 and V2.
the model presented in this paper, which is based on the deep belief networks, is capable to model the V1 responses and the V2 responses.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sparse deep belief net model can be used to learn a hierarchical structure from unlabeled images, and that the learned structure is similar to the one observed in visual cortex.

our sparse deep belief net model is able to learn a hierarchical representation of the input data that is both sparse (in terms of the number of active nodes in each layer), and also hierarchically structured (in terms of its organization into multiple layers).

we have developed a model that learns the receptive fields in V1, and the correlations in V2, without the need for labeled data, and without the need for any prior knowledge of the receptive fields in the visual cortex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the deep belief network framework, with a sparse constraint, can learn features that are similar to those found in V2.
the sparse deep belief network is a good model for V2, and that it may also be a good model for other higher cortical visual areas.
deep learning algorithms, when appropriately modified, can learn higher-order features in a principled manner, which is a step towards building a biologically inspired theory of vision.
